summary: Describes an extension to the LDAP Modify operation that adds an increment capability. It is useful in provisioning, especially with the assertion control and the pre-read or post-read controls. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A bump-the-counter button: add one to a number in the book without reading it and rewriting it.

questions: how to increment counter in ldap
subtitle: Add one to a directory attribute without reading it first.

tldr.problem: LDAP has no direct way to increment a numeric attribute. Clients must read the value, modify it, and write it back, which is slow and fails if another client changes the value in between.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4525 adds an increment operation to LDAP Modify requests. A client sends a single command to add a number to an existing attribute value.
tldr.outcome: Applications can atomically increment counters and IDs without read-modify-write races. This is especially useful with LDAP assertion controls to test-and-increment in one operation.

today: RFC 4525 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful extension for LDAP implementations that need atomic increment operations in provisioning and ID management.

sections.title: The Problem With Incrementing
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is how applications read and write a directory of people, machines and objects. It has a Modify operation to change values, but no built-in way to increment a numeric attribute.

Today, if you want to increment a counter (like the next ID to assign), you must read the old value, add one to it, and write it back. But between reading and writing, another client might do the same thing, and both will write the same new value. The RFC calls this the read-modify-write problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a notebook with a counter. To increment it, you read it (say it says 10), write 11, and close the book. But another person might do the same at the same moment, and you both end up writing 11 instead of getting 10 and 11.

sections.title: The Increment Operation
sections.content:
RFC 4525 extends the LDAP Modify request with a new operation type: increment (value 3). When a client sends an increment request, the server adds the supplied number to all existing values of that attribute.

The attribute must hold integer values (or other increment-able types). The client supplies exactly one value to add. If the attribute does not exist or holds multiple values, or if the value is not a number, the server returns an error. The whole operation is atomic—it either succeeds completely or fails completely, with no partial state.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the directory: 'Take the uidNumber and add 1.' The directory does it all at once. If anything goes wrong (like the number is a name, not a number), it rejects the whole thing.

sections.title: Server Support and Signaling
sections.content:
Servers that support this feature publish an object identifier (OID) 1.3.6.1.1.14 in their 'supportedFeatures' attribute, which clients can read from the root directory entry. Clients that support the feature should not use it unless they know the server supports it.

Servers that do not support it will treat the increment operation as an unknown value and return a protocol error. This ensures forward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers that can do this announce it, so clients know it's safe to ask. If a server doesn't support it, it says 'I don't know that operation' and you have to do it the old way.

sections.title: LDIF Representation
sections.content: The LDAP Data Interchange Format (LDIF) is a text format for bulk directory changes. RFC 4525 extends LDIF to represent increment requests using the keyword 'increment', followed by the attribute name and the value to add. For example: 'increment: uidNumber' followed by 'uidNumber: 1' tells the directory to add 1 to the uidNumber of an entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The text format for directory changes gets a new command: 'increment'. You write the field name and what to add, and the directory handles it.

sections.title: Status and Use Cases
sections.content: RFC 4525 is informational, meaning it describes a feature but does not define an Internet standard. The RFC works best when combined with the LDAP pre-read or post-read control extensions (RFC 4527) to let the client see the value before or after the increment, and with the LDAP assertion control (RFC 4528) to test a condition and increment only if it is true. These combinations are useful in provisioning applications where you want to generate unique IDs or track quota usage atomically.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a helpful feature that works especially well when paired with other LDAP tools that let you read the result and check conditions. It is useful for systems that hand out ID numbers and need to track how many have been given out.
